1061.event_title: The Rochdale Pioneers open their own co-operative store
1061.event: Twenty-eight working people of Rochdale, many of them weavers, pooled their own small savings to open a co-operative store at 31 Toad Lane on 21 December 1844, stocked with modest supplies of butter, sugar, flour, oatmeal and candles. At first it opened only two evenings a week, but within months it was open five days a week. The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers set out principles such as open membership and democratic control that became the model for the modern co-operative movement.
1061.explanation: Rather than depend on others' help, a group of poor workers met their own needs by joining their resources, and their example spread around the world.
1061.tie_back: The kural says that not asking at all, even of the kindest givers, is worth ten million times more, and the Rochdale Pioneers chose to provide for themselves through their own pooled earnings.
1061._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the Pioneers embody self-reliance, but the sources do not record them refusing any particular offer of help.

1062.event_title: New Zealand passes the Old-age Pensions Act
1062.event: Richard Seddon's Liberal government passed the Old-age Pensions Act in 1898, the first such scheme in the British Empire and paid for from general taxation. It gave a small, means-tested pension of up to 18 pounds a year to people aged 65 or over who had lived long in New Zealand and were judged to be of good character, though it shamefully excluded Chinese and other Asian residents.
1062.explanation: The act treated support for the elderly poor as a public responsibility rather than leaving them to beg or to rely on charity, and it is regarded as the birth of social security in New Zealand.
1062.tie_back: The kural angrily rejects any order of the world in which people must beg to live, and New Zealand's pension law was an early attempt to change that order so that the old and poor need not beg.
1062._accuracy_note: Next-best: the kural is an imprecation against a world that makes people beg; the act is a practical reform in that spirit, not a dramatisation of the curse.

1063.event_title: South Korea launches the Saemaul Undong self-help movement
1063.event: In 1970 South Korea launched Saemaul Undong, the New Village Movement, a rural development campaign built on the principles of diligence, self-help and cooperation, in which villagers worked together to improve their own communities. In 2013 UNESCO inscribed the movement's archives on its Memory of the World Register, noting that the campaign helped Korea move from being one of the world's poorest countries toward becoming a major economy.
1063.explanation: The movement is widely studied as an example of a poor country reducing want through organised local effort, and its methods have been shared with other developing nations.
1063.tie_back: The kural says there is no greater folly than thinking the misery of want can be cured by begging instead of effort, and Saemaul Undong was founded on curing rural poverty through villagers' own work.
1063._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for effort over dependence; the movement was government-led and its results are presented most strongly by official Korean sources.

1064.event_title: Garibaldi refuses all rewards and returns to his farm on Caprera
1064.event: After his Expedition of the Thousand conquered Sicily and Naples in 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi handed his dictatorship over southern Italy to King Victor Emmanuel II. He turned down all the rewards offered to him and went back at once to his small farm on the rocky island of Caprera, where he had settled to farm some years before.
1064.explanation: Having won half a kingdom, Garibaldi accepted nothing for himself, and his refusal became a celebrated example of selflessness in the Italian Risorgimento.
1064.tie_back: The kural praises the nobility that will not consent to take from others even when one has little, a greatness the whole world cannot contain, and Garibaldi chose a modest farm over every reward a grateful king could give.
1064._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of noble refusal, though Garibaldi was not destitute and declined rewards rather than refused to beg.

1065.event: Jean-Francois Millet showed The Gleaners at the Paris Salon of 1857. The painting depicts three peasant women bent over a harvested field gathering the stray ears of wheat left by the harvesters, which the rural poor were customarily allowed to collect, while the abundant harvest is gathered in the distance. The Musee d'Orsay, which holds the painting, notes that Millet gave the women an emblematic dignity, and some critics of the time read the picture as a political statement.
1065.explanation: Millet presented the poor winning their meagre bread by their own labour as worthy of the grandeur usually reserved for history painting.
1065.tie_back: The kural says that even gruel thin as water is sweetest when it is earned by one's own effort, and The Gleaners honours poor women gathering a scanty harvest with their own hands rather than asking for it.
1065._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the painting shows hard-won food gathered by labour, but it is an artwork and says nothing directly about the sweetness of eating it.

1066.event_title: Booker T. Washington describes the burden of raising money for Tuskegee
1066.place: Tuskegee, Alabama, and the northern United States
1066.event: In the chapter Raising Money in his autobiography Up From Slavery (1901), Booker T. Washington described years of travelling to ask northern donors for the funds that kept Tuskegee Institute running beyond its small state grant. He recalled walking through a cold storm in Stamford, Connecticut, to call on a possible donor who heard him out and gave nothing, and he explained that he kept to the rule of doing his duty whether or not money came.
1066.explanation: Washington's account shows that even asking for a worthy cause on behalf of others was hard, wearing and often fruitless work.
1066.tie_back: The kural says that even asking water for a thirsty cow is lowering to the tongue, and Washington's honest account of soliciting money for his students shows how heavy asking remains even for the noblest purpose.
1066._accuracy_note: Next-best: Washington describes the difficulty of asking for a good cause but presents it as duty rather than as degrading.

1067.event_title: Alexandre Petion equips Simon Bolivar for a new campaign
1067.event: After defeats on the mainland and a period of exile in Jamaica, Simon Bolivar went to Haiti at the end of 1815. President Alexandre Petion supplied him with arms, munitions, provisions and men for a new expedition against Spanish rule, asking in return only that Bolivar abolish slavery in the lands he freed. Bolivar sailed for Venezuela in 1816 proclaiming the abolition of slavery as one of his aims.
1067.explanation: Historians regard Petion's open-handed help as decisive for the revival of the independence struggle in northern South America.
1067.tie_back: The kural begs those who must ask to ask only of people who do not hide what they have, and Bolivar found in Petion a giver who gave freely, asking nothing for himself.
1067._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows asking of an open-handed giver, but the sources do not document Bolivar choosing Petion after being refused by others.

1068.event_title: Japan's racial equality proposal is blocked at the Paris Peace Conference
1068.event: At the Paris Peace Conference Japan proposed adding to the Covenant of the League of Nations a clause affirming the equality of nations and the fair treatment of their nationals. On 11 April 1919 a majority of the League of Nations Commission voted in favour, but the chairman, US President Woodrow Wilson, ruled that it required unanimous support, and with Britain and Australia opposed, the clause was dropped.
1068.explanation: The rejection was deeply resented in Japan and is often cited as a turning point in Japan's relations with the Western powers.
1068.tie_back: The kural compares asking to a frail little boat that splits apart when it strikes the rock of refusal, and Japan's appeal, though supported by a majority, broke on a single ruling.
1068._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: a diplomatic proposal rather than a plea in need, and Japan's own aims in making it are debated by historians.

1069.event: Troubled by a parliamentary report on child labour, Charles Dickens first planned a factual pamphlet but instead wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks, publishing it on 19 December 1843; the first printing of 6,000 copies sold out by Christmas Eve. In the story the miser Ebenezer Scrooge coldly turns away gentlemen collecting for the poor, before being shown the suffering his hardness causes and the joy of generosity.
1069.explanation: The book became one of the best-loved stories in English and fixed Scrooge's name as the type of the person who refuses help to those in need.
1069.tie_back: The kural says the heart melts at the thought of those who must beg but is crushed at the thought of those who refuse them, and Dickens wrote his story out of pity for the poor and made the refuser its central figure.
1069._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of compassion for the needy set against horror at the refuser, though it is a work of fiction.

1070.event_title: George III refuses to receive the Olive Branch Petition
1070.event: In July 1775 the Second Continental Congress adopted the Olive Branch Petition, written chiefly by John Dickinson, professing loyalty to King George III and asking him to help end the conflict with the colonies. Richard Penn and Arthur Lee delivered it in London, but the king would not receive it, having already proclaimed on 23 August 1775 that the colonies were in open rebellion. Congress made no further attempt at reconciliation and declared independence the following July.
1070.explanation: The refusal closed the last door to reconciliation, and within a few years Britain lost the thirteen colonies.
1070.tie_back: The kural asks where the life of the refuser can hide when a refusal crushes the one who asks, and the king's refusal of the colonists' petition led to the loss of Britain's own empire in America.
1070._accuracy_note: Next-best: the colonists were petitioners rather than beggars, and the link between the refusal and Britain's later loss is interpretive.
